questions.prompt: What is an optional in Swift, and why does Swift require optionals to represent missing values? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines an optional as a type that wraps either a real value or nil
Explains that non-optional types in Swift can never be nil
Mentions that optionals prevent null pointer crashes by requiring explicit handling at compile time

questions.modelAnswer: An optional in Swift is a type that can hold either a real value or nil. Swift enforces that standard non-optional types can never be nil. This design eliminates null pointer crashes at compile time. By forcing developers to handle potential nil values explicitly, Swift makes code much safer and more reliable.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: The Basics (Optionals)

questions.prompt: Compare if let and guard let for unwrapping optionals in Swift. When should you choose each? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that if let binds the unwrapped constant only inside the conditional block
Explains that guard let keeps the unwrapped constant in the outer scope and requires an early exit
Explains when to choose each (e.g., guard let for early exits / guard clauses to avoid indentation; if let for optional branching)

questions.modelAnswer: Both if let and guard let unwrap optionals safely. With if let, the unwrapped constant is accessible only inside the if block. In contrast, guard let requires an early exit in the else block and keeps the unwrapped value available for the remainder of the function. Use guard let to validate prerequisites early and prevent deep nesting, and use if let when you need simple conditional branching.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: The Basics (Optionals)

questions.prompt: How does the nil-coalescing operator (??) work, and what advantages does it offer over forced unwrapping? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that ?? returns the wrapped value if present, or a fallback default value if nil
Explains that it produces a non-optional value safely without runtime crashes
Contrasts this with forced unwrapping (!) which crashes immediately on nil

questions.modelAnswer: The nil-coalescing operator ?? unwraps an optional if it contains a value, or provides a default fallback value if the optional is nil. Unlike forced unwrapping with !, which triggers an immediate fatal runtime crash on nil, ?? is completely safe. It allows an application to recover gracefully from missing data while producing a clean non-optional value.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: The Basics (Optionals)

questions.prompt: Why is forced unwrapping with ! considered an anti-pattern in production Swift code? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that forced unwrapping causes a fatal runtime crash if the value is nil
Explains that it bypasses Swift's compile-time safety guarantees
Recommends safe alternatives like if let, guard let, or ??

questions.modelAnswer: Forced unwrapping with ! bypasses Swift's compile-time safety mechanisms. If the optional contains nil when evaluated, the application terminates immediately with a fatal error. Even if a value seems guaranteed, code changes or concurrency issues can cause unexpected nil values. In production apps, developers should use safe techniques like if let, guard let, or nil-coalescing instead.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: The Basics (Optionals)

questions.prompt: How is Optional implemented in the Swift standard library, and how does its enum structure work? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Optional is an enumeration with cases .none and .some(Wrapped)
States that .none represents nil, while .some holds the wrapped value
Mentions that syntax like Type? is syntactic sugar for Optional<Type>

questions.modelAnswer: In the Swift standard library, Optional is implemented as a generic enumeration with two cases: .none and .some(Wrapped). The .none case represents nil, while the .some case stores the wrapped payload. Writing Type? is simply syntactic sugar for Optional<Type>. Because Optional is a standard value type, it benefits from Swift's pattern matching and protocol conformances.
